figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 1. Typical Examples of natural products derived from fungi. Fungi produce 
a variety of natural products, such as non-ribosomal peptides penicillin G and 
cyclosporine A, polyketides lovastatin and mycophenolic acid, terpenes pleu­
romutilin and alkaloids psilocybin.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 2. Strategies for exploring natural products from fungi. Various strategies 
have been developed for activating cryptic BGCs in microbes. The one strain 
many compounds (OSMAC) strategy explores the potential of one particular 
fungal strain for producing natural products by varying the cultivation pa­
rameters. Replacing the promoter of cryptic BGC genes with highly expressed 
promoters represent another effective strategy for activating silent BGCs. 
Activating or enhancing the transcription of BGC genes is often achieved by 
modification of chromatin, manipulating global and/or pathway specific 
regulator. Developing a platform for heterologous expression of fungal BGCs 
represents another versatile tool for exploration and efficient production of 
fungal natural products, especially for those derived from uncultivatable fungi 
or from fungi that lack genetic manipulation tools.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 3. Strategies for biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) assembly and transfer 
used for fungal heterologous expression. Various approaches have been 
employed for fungal BGC cloning and expression in heterologous hosts. (A) In 
the separate cloning and sequential transfer method, each gene was separately 
cloned and sequentially integrated at defined or random loci; (B) Intact fungal 
BGCs can be assembled by in vitro assembly methods including USER™ cloning, 
Golden gate assembly, Gibson assembly, Gateway® assembly and fusion PCR; 
(C) Yeast homologous recombination can be employed for assembling multiple 
DNA fragments of BGCs with homologous arms between each other and the 
vectors; (D) Intact fungal BGCs can be captured in cosmids or fungal artificial 
chromosomes (FACs) and transferred into heterologous host; (E) Recently 
developed CRISPR-Cas9 tools can be used for assembling BGCs fragments with 
homologous arms directly in heterologous fungal host; (F) Multiple genes of 
BGCs can be organized in polycistronic form using 2A peptide.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 4. Strategies used for increasing the precursor acetyl-CoA and malony-CoA 
supply for polyketide synthesis in fungal hosts. The pyruvate dehydrogenase 
complex (PDH) can be overexpressed in the cytoplasm, enhancing cytosol 
acetyl-CoA supply. In the PDH bypass pathway, pyruvate is converted to 
acetaldehyde by pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC) and then to acetate by aldehyde 
dehydrogenase (ALD) and to acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA synthase (ACS). Citrate 
derived from peroxisome or mitochondria can be converted to acetyl-CoA by 
cytosol citrate lyase (ACL). Enhancing β-oxidation and/or peroxisome prolif­
eration are also reported to be beneficial for polyketide synthesis. Disrupting 
the acetyl-CoA consumption pathways by blocking glyoxylate cycle, lipid syn­
thesis and ergosterol synthesis are also employed to increase the acetyl- 
CoA level.
